title: Research Explained #17 — How Would We Know Where a Signal Actually Went? — Tracing Light Through Curved Spacetime
html:
A receiver detects a pulse. It has an arrival time, an incoming direction, a frequency spectrum, and perhaps an identifiable pattern. But none of those measurements comes with a complete map of the route.

In curved spacetime, reconstructing that route means comparing observations with predictions from a specified physical model. Sometimes several routes fit. Sometimes the data constrain a family of geometries rather than a unique path. The honest answer may be: we know which models remain consistent with the measurements, but we have not uniquely reconstructed the journey.

This matters for ordinary radio links and astronomy. It also matters for Beyond the Light Barrier (BTLB): before interpreting a proposed communication channel or propulsion geometry, we must specify how signals connect a sender to a receiver.

Evidence boundary: General relativity and observed gravitational lensing provide established foundations. Hypothetical wormhole or warp geometries are a separate theoretical question. This article reports no new BTLB simulation or physical experiment. Project-status statements below refer specifically to the supplied Research State v1.11, not to an independently established later status.

1. A straight line depends on the map

In general relativity, freely propagating light in vacuum is described, in the geometric-optics limit, by null geodesics. “Geometric optics” means that the wavelength is short compared with the relevant curvature and background-variation scales. Diffraction, interference, plasma dispersion, scattering, and absorption can require a wave or material model instead of ray tracing alone. [1]

A geodesic is the spacetime generalization of an unforced straight path. Its appearance on a coordinate map can bend. A different choice of coordinates can change the drawn curve without changing the physical observation.

That distinction prevents a common mistake: a coordinate speed or a visually shortened line is not, by itself, a measured violation of the local speed of light.

2. What “null” means—and what it does not mean

Use metric signature (−,+,+,+), with coordinates x0 = ct and three spatial coordinates, all in metres in a local Cartesian chart. The spacetime interval is

(1)   ds2 = Σμ,ν=03 gμν dxμ dxν.

The metric gμν specifies spacetime geometry; Greek indices label its four coordinates. A light ray satisfies ds2 = 0. Locally, where freely falling coordinates make the metric Minkowskian at an event, this becomes

(2)   0 = −c2dt2 + dx2 + dy2 + dz2.

Thus the local spatial distance divided by local time is c, the vacuum speed of light. Each term has units of square metres. “Zero interval” does not mean zero travel distance or instantaneous transmission. Light has no rest frame in which we can place a photon clock. [2]

In engineering terms: the metric supplies the geometry and clock relationships. The null condition restricts the allowed lightlike directions. We still need an equation telling us how the direction evolves.

3. The equation that traces the ray

For an affine parameter λ, write kμ = dxμ/dλ. The ray equations are

(3)   dxμ/dλ = kμ,
dkμ/dλ = −Γμαβ kαkβ,
gμνkμkν = 0.

Repeated indices are summed. The connection coefficients Γ are calculated from the metric:

Γμαβ = ½ gμσ(∂αgσβ + ∂βgσα − ∂σgαβ).

Here gμσ is the inverse metric and ∂α is differentiation with respect to xα. We may choose λ in metres; then k is dimensionless and Γ has units of inverse metres in the stated chart, so both sides of the second equation have units of inverse metres. λ is not a photon's proper time. [2]

In engineering terms: choose a geometry, a launch event, and a launch direction; then advance position and direction together. In a flat Cartesian vacuum metric, Γ vanishes and the calculation must recover straight rays. The null condition alone would not enforce geodesic motion.

4. Gravitational lensing can provide more than one route

A gravitational lens can produce multiple images of one source. In ray language, distinct null geodesics can connect an emission event to different reception events on an observer's worldline. Their travel times need not agree.

For a weak, isolated, approximately pointlike mass M, the leading general-relativistic deflection is

(4)   α̂ ≈ 4GM/(c2b).

G is Newton's gravitational constant and b the impact parameter relative to the unperturbed asymptotic ray, in metres. The angle is dimensionless, expressed in radians. This weak-deflection approximation requires b ≫ GM/c2 and suitable distant endpoints; it is not a strong-field or arbitrary-metric formula. It vanishes as M → 0 or b → ∞. Multiple images depend on the lens and alignment; the formula alone does not guarantee them. [3]

Different images of a variable source may show matching features at different times. Kundić and colleagues used the delayed appearance of a feature in the lensed quasar 0957+561A,B to test a predicted image delay. This is observational evidence about a lens system, not evidence for an engineered shortcut. [4]

Two photons taking different routes are not one photon being tracked twice. A received signal is reconstructed from many detections and a propagation model.

5. Shapiro delay: timing contains information about geometry

Shapiro proposed testing relativity through the additional radar travel time associated with a gravitating body. [5] For a static spherical mass, the leading weak-field, one-way coordinate light time can be written

(5)   tr − te ≈ R/c + ΔtSh,
ΔtSh = (1+γ)GM/c3 ln[(re+rr+R)/(re+rr−R)].

Here re and rr are endpoint distances from the mass, R is their Euclidean coordinate separation, and γ is the dimensionless parametrized post-Newtonian spatial-curvature parameter, equal to 1 in general relativity. This first-order expression uses standard weak-field isotropic coordinates. Its logarithm is dimensionless and GM/c3 has units of seconds. It assumes a nonocculted weak-field path; it is not valid arbitrarily near a horizon or for arbitrary moving masses. Higher-order corrections can matter in precision work. [6]

The correction tends to zero as M → 0. A round-trip observable requires separate outward and return legs, with endpoint motion and any turnaround delay included; blindly doubling a one-way expression can be wrong.

Cassini's radio-link experiment tested relativistic propagation using frequency changes associated with the changing gravitational delay. It did not watch a signal continuously along its route. [7] Nor should Shapiro delay be described as light locally slowing below c. The coordinate timing contribution and its separation from a “flat” baseline depend on the adopted model; measured clock readings are the quantities to predict.

In a lens system, relative arrival delays generally contain both geometrical and gravitational contributions. Timing alone is not a ruler measuring the spatial length of a route. [3]

6. Moving endpoints turn tracing into an interception problem

A receiver is not a fixed dot on a map. Let ze(τe) and zr(τr) be the sender's and receiver's worldlines, parametrized by their own proper times in seconds. A connecting ray must satisfy

(6)   x(λe) = ze(τe),   x(λr) = zr(τr).

For a specified emission event, the launch direction and reception time may both be unknown. One must solve for a ray that meets the receiver where it will be. A configuration can have no connecting ray in a specified time window, one, or several. This is a boundary-value problem, rather than merely a drawing between two present positions. [1]

A useful flat-spacetime check can be derived directly. Suppose a receiver starts at distance L and recedes in a straight line at constant speed v, where 0 ≤ v < c, in the sender's inertial frame. For a pulse launched at t = 0, interception requires ct = L + vt, hence

(7)   tr = L/(c−v).

This article's elementary analytic check is Category 6, not a simulation. It reduces to L/c at v = 0 and grows without bound as v approaches c. The endpoint motion lengthens the interception time even though light's local speed remains c.

Frequency adds another constraint. If qμ is the electromagnetic phase wavevector and uμ = dzμ/dτ is an observer's four-velocity, then

(8)   ω = −uμqμ,   ωr/ωe = (uμqμ)r/(uμqμ)e.

The wave covector qμ is the gradient of dimensionless phase, in inverse metres for our length coordinates; u has units of metres per second. Thus ω has units of radians per second. Its normalization is fixed by the emitted frequency, unlike an arbitrarily normalized ray tangent. Doppler and gravitational frequency shifts are contained in the endpoint contractions and intervening propagation. This invariant measurement rule is part of the relativistic ray description. [1]

7. What would let us distinguish the routes?

A practical inference would compare a set of candidate models against several observables together:

  • Timing: emission tags, reception tags, clock calibration, and relative delays.
  • Direction: incoming angle in the receiver's local frame, with pointing uncertainty.
  • Frequency and phase: source stability, receiver motion, propagation shifts, and instrument response.
  • Signal identity: matching encoded content or repeatable source features, with false-association tests.
  • Endpoint and environment data: trajectories, intervening mass estimates, plasma, reflections, multipath propagation, and interference.

This is a proposed measurement-and-analysis strategy, not a report that BTLB has performed it. One-way timing also needs a declared synchronization convention and clock model. A single receiver can directly measure a round-trip proper-time interval, but interpreting the two legs still needs a propagation model.

The test should predict observations, fit nuisance parameters, quantify uncertainty, and compare conventional alternatives. Different mass distributions or endpoint histories may remain indistinguishable with limited data. A mismatch can expose an inaccurate clock, an incorrect trajectory, a missing propagation effect, or a failed geometry assumption; it does not automatically establish new physics.

8. What changes for a hypothetical geometry?

The same equations can be applied to a specified hypothetical metric, provided its domain, smoothness, coordinate patches, and boundary conditions are defined. Published examples include Alcubierre's warp metric and Perlick's analysis of lensing in an Ellis wormhole geometry. These are mathematical investigations; neither source establishes an engineered spacetime channel. [8] [9]

For a time-dependent candidate, a static lens approximation may fail. Horizons, inaccessible regions, missing connecting rays, or coordinate singularities must be examined rather than hidden by a visually attractive trajectory. A horizon cannot be declared from a coordinate plot alone.

The conditional question is: if this geometry and these endpoints were specified, what would a receiver measure? Answering that does not answer whether the geometry can exist, be generated, remain stable, be controlled, or respect the required causal constraints. Those are additional physics questions. A proposed shortcut must be compared with a conventional reference under explicitly matched operational conditions, not declared FTL from a coordinate line length.

Ray tracing also cannot establish a complete communication link budget. Detectability, bandwidth, wave transmission, noise, diffraction, and source and receiver coupling still matter.

9. Where this fits in BTLB

The Shared Field Map v1.0 explicitly proposes, in Comparison Queue Priority 4, a shared null-ray and moving-endpoint benchmark suite on known spacetimes before speculative geometries, including clock, frequency, phase, and angle predictions. It is a proposed comparison program, not evidence of a completed benchmark suite. The map describes itself as a selective bibliography and does not claim methodological uniqueness. [P1]

Research State v1.11 identifies null-geodesic/photon propagation, moving endpoints, synchronization, causal structure, and source realism as shared WC/WD problems (§36.6). Sharing an analysis does not merge the communication and propulsion conclusions. The same record classifies WC-MGT-1 carrier propagation as Category 7, internally reproduced/cross-validated, in an assumed geometry (§4.1). It does not establish a physically generated wormhole or a completed version of the proposed ray suite. Its retained low-frequency electromagnetic scan found no useful resonance in the scanned configuration. That negative result must remain part of the account. [P4]

Consistent with those documents, a sensible proposed implementation sequence for this article is:

  1. Flat vacuum baseline: stationary and moving endpoints; recover straight rays, ordinary interception times, and special-relativistic frequency shifts.
  2. Established curved reference: a specified Schwarzschild exterior; recover weak-field deflection and delay in their valid limits, then assess stronger-field behavior with appropriate coordinates.
  3. Numerical verification: refine integration tolerances; monitor a normalized null-constraint residual and applicable conserved quantities; vary launch guesses to search for distinct connecting paths. A small null residual alone does not prove correct interception or complete path discovery.
  4. Frozen reproduction package: preserve metric/version, units, endpoint worldlines, emission conditions, domain and boundaries, solver and tolerances, search strategy, outputs, uncertainties, and failed or missing connections.
  5. Conditional extensions: only then compare explicitly hypothetical geometries, keeping physical source, stability, and causality gates separate.

This sequence is an editorial proposal grounded in the map and governance documents, not an adopted new BTLB model or a claim that these runs have occurred.

Research Method v1.2 requires claim traceability, checkable mathematics, preserved negative results, and separation of computation from physical evidence (§§2–3, 6–7, 9–12, 20). Verification Roadmap v1.1 requires meaningful independence before Category 8 and a predicted observable, detector response, controls, and uncertainty budget before physical precursor development (§§2, 5, 11). Cross-platform execution or another internal solver is not, on its own, independent scientific reproduction. [P2] [P3]

10. What would count as evidence?

Evidence distinctions used in this article
Claim or activity Classification and limit
Observed lens images and measured radio-link effects in the external literature Category 1: established observational/experimental evidence within the supported scope; not BTLB experimental results.
General-relativistic vacuum null-geodesic framework Category 2: accepted theory within its applicable domain.
Published hypothetical warp or wormhole geometry Category 3: published speculative theory as to physical realization; mathematical consistency does not establish existence.
A new BTLB conjecture about a channel Category 4: project hypothesis; none is established by this article.
A proposed link, apparatus, or benchmark architecture Category 5 when an engineering concept; a proposal is not a measured capability.
A derived interception time or approximate delay Category 6: analytic calculation, conditional on assumptions.
A numerically integrated ray Category 7: computational result, if actually run and documented; this article supplies no such new result.
A meaningfully independent reproduction Category 8 only after independence and comparison are documented; it still would not establish physical realization of an assumed geometry.
A calibrated physical test Category 9: experimental result only for the observable actually tested, with controls and uncertainty; mechanism attribution remains a separate inference.

In the supplied Research State v1.11, Category 8 independent scientific reproduction remains none, and Category 9 physical experimental evidence remains none. No BTLB result in that record establishes FTL communication, FTL propulsion, a physical traversable wormhole, anomalous gravity, or engineered FTL spacetime. [P4]

Knowing where a signal went is an inference built from geometry, endpoint motion, calibrated observations, and tests against alternatives. The useful research milestone is a prediction that survives those checks—including the possibility that the proposed route is absent or observationally indistinguishable from an ordinary one.

References and further reading

External references support the physics or observations indicated above. They do not verify a BTLB model.

  1. V. Perlick, “Gravitational Lensing from a Spacetime Perspective,” Living Reviews in Relativity 7, 9 (2004). doi:10.12942/lrr-2004-9. Relativistic ray and observer framework.
  2. S. M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity (1997), especially the geometry/geodesic discussion. arXiv:gr-qc/9712019. Pedagogical theoretical reference.
  3. R. Narayan and M. Bartelmann, Lectures on Gravitational Lensing (1996; revised 1997). arXiv:astro-ph/9606001. Weak-deflection and lens-delay formulations.
  4. T. Kundić et al., “A Robust Determination of the Time Delay in 0957+561A,B and a Measurement of the Global Value of Hubble's Constant,” Astrophysical Journal 482, 75–82 (1997). doi:10.1086/304147; author manuscript.
  5. I. I. Shapiro, “Fourth Test of General Relativity,” Physical Review Letters 13, 789–791 (1964). doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.789. Original proposed timing test.
  6. N. Ashby and B. Bertotti, “Accurate light-time correction due to a gravitating mass,” Classical and Quantum Gravity 27, 145013 (2010). doi:10.1088/0264-9381/27/14/145013; author manuscript.
  7. B. Bertotti, L. Iess, and P. Tortora, “A test of general relativity using radio links with the Cassini spacecraft,” Nature 425, 374–376 (2003). doi:10.1038/nature01997.
  8. M. Alcubierre, “The warp drive: hyper-fast travel within general relativity,” Classical and Quantum Gravity 11, L73–L77 (1994). doi:10.1088/0264-9381/11/5/001; author manuscript. Speculative physical geometry, not demonstrated propulsion.
  9. V. Perlick, “Exact gravitational lens equation in spherically symmetric and static spacetimes,” Physical Review D 69, 064017 (2004). doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.69.064017. Includes a hypothetical Ellis-wormhole example.

    Horizons, inaccessible regions, missing connecting rays, or coordinate
    singularities must be examined rather than hidden by a visually attractive
    trajectory. A horizon cannot be declared from a coordinate plot alone.
  

  

    The conditional question is: if this geometry and these
    endpoints were specified, what would a receiver measure? Answering that does
    not answer whether the geometry can exist, be generated, remain stable, be
    controlled, or respect the required causal constraints. Those are additional
    physics questions. A proposed shortcut must be compared with a conventional
    reference under explicitly matched operational conditions, not declared FTL
    from a coordinate line length.
  

  

    Ray tracing also cannot establish a complete communication link budget.
    Detectability, bandwidth, wave transmission, noise, diffraction, and source
    and receiver coupling still matter.
  

  
9. Where this fits in BTLB

  

    The Shared Field Map v1.0 explicitly proposes, in
    Comparison Queue Priority 4, a shared null-ray and moving-endpoint benchmark
    suite on known spacetimes before speculative geometries, including clock,
    frequency, phase, and angle predictions. It is a proposed comparison
    program, not evidence of a completed benchmark suite. The map describes
    itself as a selective bibliography and does not claim methodological
    uniqueness. [P1]
  

  

    Research State v1.11 identifies null-geodesic/photon
    propagation, moving endpoints, synchronization, causal structure, and source
    realism as shared WC/WD problems (§36.6). Sharing an analysis does not merge
    the communication and propulsion conclusions. The same record classifies
    WC-MGT-1 carrier propagation as Category 7, internally
    reproduced/cross-validated, in an assumed geometry (§4.1). It does not
    establish a physically generated wormhole or a completed version of the
    proposed ray suite. Its retained low-frequency electromagnetic scan found no
    useful resonance in the scanned configuration. That negative result must
    remain part of the account. [P4]
  

  

    Consistent with those documents, a sensible
    proposed implementation sequence for this article is:
  

  

    
- 
      Flat vacuum baseline: stationary and moving endpoints;
      recover straight rays, ordinary interception times, and
      special-relativistic frequency shifts.
    

    
- 
      Established curved reference: a specified Schwarzschild
      exterior; recover weak-field deflection and delay in their valid limits,
      then assess stronger-field behavior with appropriate coordinates.
    

    
- 
      Numerical verification: refine integration tolerances;
      monitor a normalized null-constraint residual and applicable conserved
      quantities; vary launch guesses to search for distinct connecting paths. A
      small null residual alone does not prove correct interception or complete
      path discovery.
    

    
- 
      Frozen reproduction package: preserve metric/version,
      units, endpoint worldlines, emission conditions, domain and boundaries,
      solver and tolerances, search strategy, outputs, uncertainties, and failed
      or missing connections.
    

    
- 
      Conditional extensions: only then compare explicitly
      hypothetical geometries, keeping physical source, stability, and causality
      gates separate.
    

  

  

    This sequence is an editorial proposal grounded in the map and governance
    documents, not an adopted new BTLB model or a claim that these runs have
    occurred.
  

  

    Research Method v1.2 requires claim traceability, checkable
    mathematics, preserved negative results, and separation of computation from
    physical evidence (§§2–3, 6–7, 9–12, 20).
    Verification Roadmap v1.1 requires meaningful independence
    before Category 8 and a predicted observable, detector response, controls,
    and uncertainty budget before physical precursor development (§§2, 5, 11).
    Cross-platform execution or another internal solver is not, on its own,
    independent scientific reproduction. [P2]
    [P3]
  

  
10. What would count as evidence?

  

    

      
        Evidence distinctions used in this article
      
      
        

          Claim or activity	
          Classification and limit	
        

      
      
        

          
            Observed lens images and measured radio-link effects in the external
            literature
          	
          
            Category 1: established observational/experimental evidence within
            the supported scope; not BTLB experimental results.
          	
        

        

          General-relativistic vacuum null-geodesic framework	
          Category 2: accepted theory within its applicable domain.	
        

        

          Published hypothetical warp or wormhole geometry	
          
            Category 3: published speculative theory as to physical realization;
            mathematical consistency does not establish existence.
          	
        

        

          A new BTLB conjecture about a channel	
          
            Category 4: project hypothesis; none is established by this article.
          	
        

        

          A proposed link, apparatus, or benchmark architecture	
          
            Category 5 when an engineering concept; a proposal is not a measured
            capability.
          	
        

        

          A derived interception time or approximate delay	
          Category 6: analytic calculation, conditional on assumptions.	
        

        

          A numerically integrated ray	
          
            Category 7: computational result, if actually run and documented;
            this article supplies no such new result.
          	
        

        

          A meaningfully independent reproduction	
          
            Category 8 only after independence and comparison are documented; it
            still would not establish physical realization of an assumed
            geometry.
          	
        

        

          A calibrated physical test	
          
            Category 9: experimental result only for the observable actually
            tested, with controls and uncertainty; mechanism attribution remains
            a separate inference.
          	
        

      
    

  

  

    In the supplied Research State v1.11, Category 8
    independent scientific reproduction remains none, and
    Category 9 physical experimental evidence remains none. No
    BTLB result in that record establishes FTL communication, FTL propulsion, a
    physical traversable wormhole, anomalous gravity, or engineered FTL
    spacetime. [P4]
  

  

    Knowing where a signal went is an inference built from geometry, endpoint
    motion, calibrated observations, and tests against alternatives. The useful
    research milestone is a prediction that survives those checks—including the
    possibility that the proposed route is absent or observationally
    indistinguishable from an ordinary one.
